decks.title: Application of Integrals — Part 1: Area bounded by a curve
goals: Find the area between a curve and the x-axis using a definite integral
Handle curves that lie below or cross the x-axis
Use horizontal strips for curves of the form x = g(y)
Find areas under modulus, exponential and logarithmic curves, and of circles and ellipses

slides.heading: Application of Integrals, Part 1
slides.body_md: A definite integral of a non-negative function measures the area under its graph.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 1: area under a curve, curves below the axis, horizontal strips, modulus, exponential and logarithmic curves, and circles and ellipses.
visual.caption: Part 1 at a glance.

slides.narration: Welcome to the application of integrals. In this part we use definite integrals to measure the area of a region bounded by a curve and the axes or straight lines. We will meet straight lines, parabolas, cubics, modulus graphs, exponential and logarithmic curves, circles and ellipses.

slides.heading: What you will learn
bullets: Area under a curve above the axis

rows: Under $y = f(x) \ge 0$, from $x = a$ to $x = b$
Between $x = g(y) \ge 0$ and the $y$-axis, $c \le y \le d$

visual.alt: Table of area formulas: under a curve above the axis, the integral of f from a to b; for a curve below the axis, the absolute value of the integral; between a curve x equals g of y and the y-axis, the integral in y; an ellipse with semi-axes a and b has area pi a b.
visual.caption: The formulas of Part 1.

slides.narration: Here are the goals and the formulas. When the curve is above the axis the area is simply the integral. When it is below, take the absolute value. For a curve written as x in terms of y, integrate in y. An ellipse with semi-axes a and b has area pi a b.

slides.heading: Area under a curve
slides.body_md: If $f(x) \ge 0$ on $[a, b]$, the area under $y = f(x)$ from $x = a$ to $x = b$ is $\displaystyle\int_a^b f(x)\,dx$.

visual.alt: Graph of y equals x squared over 2 plus 1 on minus 0.5 to 3.2. The curve stays above the x-axis, starting at (0, 1) and passing through (2, 3); the region under it between x equal to 0 and x equal to 2 is the area being measured.
visual.caption: Area from $x = 0$ to $x = 2$: $\int_0^2 \left(\tfrac{x^2}{2} + 1\right)dx = \tfrac{10}{3}$.

slides.narration: Picture thin vertical strips under the curve, each of width d x and height f of x. Adding their areas and letting the width shrink gives the definite integral. So when the curve stays above the axis, the area between the ordinates x equals a and x equals b is just the integral from a to b.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: area under a parabola
slides.body_md: Find the area under $y = x^2 + 2x$ from $x = 0$ to $x = 2$.
bullets: The curve is above the axis on $[0, 2]$

visual.alt: Worked example table: the curve y equals x squared plus 2 x is above the axis on 0 to 2, so the area is the integral of x squared plus 2 x from 0 to 2, which is 8 over 3 plus 4, that is 20 over 3.
visual.caption: Checked by quadrature.

slides.narration: First check the sign: for x between zero and two, x squared plus two x is not negative, so the curve is above the axis. The area is the integral from zero to two. An antiderivative is x cubed over three plus x squared, which gives eight thirds plus four, that is twenty thirds.

slides.heading: Quick check: under a cubic
slides.body_md: Find the area under a cubic arc up to an ordinate.
slides.narration: Integrate x cubed from zero to two. Is the curve above the axis there?

slides.heading: Curves below the axis
slides.body_md: If $f(x) \le 0$ on $[a, b]$, the area is $\left|\displaystyle\int_a^b f(x)\,dx\right| = -\displaystyle\int_a^b f(x)\,dx$.

visual.alt: Graph of y equals x squared minus 2 x on minus 0.5 to 3. It meets the x-axis at (0, 0) and (2, 0) and dips below the axis between them; it rises to (3, 3).
visual.caption: The dip has area $\left|\int_0^2 (x^2 - 2x)\,dx\right| = \tfrac43$.

slides.narration: When the curve lies below the axis, every strip has negative height, so the integral comes out negative. An area is never negative, so take the absolute value. Here the parabola x squared minus two x dips below the axis between zero and two, and the area of the dip is four thirds.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: a curve that crosses the axis
slides.body_md: Find the area between $y = x^2 - x - 2$ and the $x$-axis for $0 \le x \le 3$.

visual.alt: Worked example table: y equals x squared minus x minus 2 is negative on 0 to 2 and positive on 2 to 3. The areas of the two pieces are 10 over 3 and 11 over 6, adding to 31 over 6.
visual.caption: Split at the zero $x = 2$.

slides.narration: Factorise: x squared minus x minus two is x minus two times x plus one. Inside the interval it changes sign only at two. Below the axis on zero to two, the piece has area ten thirds; above it on two to three, the area is eleven sixths. Add the pieces to get thirty one sixths.

slides.heading: Quick check: a full sine wave
slides.body_md: Find the total area of the two humps of a sine wave.
slides.narration: Why does the integral over a full wave give zero, and what is the area?

slides.heading: Horizontal strips
slides.body_md: For a curve given as $x = g(y)$, slice the region horizontally and integrate in $y$.

visual.alt: Table comparing strips: a vertical strip of width d x has length upper y minus lower y; a horizontal strip of width d y has length right x minus left x. Example: between x equals y squared and the y-axis for y from 0 to 2 the area is 8 over 3.
visual.caption: Choose the strip that gives one formula for the whole region.

slides.narration: Some regions are easier to slice sideways. If the boundary is written as x in terms of y, use horizontal strips of width d y. The length of a strip is the right boundary minus the left boundary, and the limits are values of y. For example, between x equals y squared and the y-axis, from y equals zero to two, the area is eight thirds.

slides.heading: Modulus curves
slides.body_md: Split at the corner, where the expression inside the modulus is zero.

visual.alt: Graph of y equals the modulus of x plus 1 on minus 3.2 to 2.2: a V shape with its corner at (minus 1, 0), rising to (minus 3, 2) on the left and to (2, 3) on the right.
visual.caption: Two triangles: $2 + 4.5 = 6.5$ square units.

slides.narration: A modulus graph has a corner where the inside is zero. On each side it is a straight line, so the region under it is made of triangles or trapeziums. For the modulus of x plus one between minus three and two, the corner is at minus one, and the two triangles give two plus four and a half.

slides.heading: Quick check: a missing limit
slides.body_md: Find the upper limit that gives a stated area under a parabola.
slides.narration: Write the area in terms of k and solve.

slides.heading: Logarithmic and exponential curves
slides.body_md: $\log x < 0$ for $0 < x < 1$, and $e^x > 0$ always.

visual.alt: Graph of y equals log x for x from 0.25 to 4. It is below the x-axis for x less than 1, crosses the axis at (1, 0), and passes through (e, 1).
visual.caption: From $x = 1$ to $x = e$ the area is $1$; to the left of $1$ the curve is below the axis.

slides.narration: The logarithm is negative for x between zero and one, crosses the axis at one, and rises slowly after that. So an area under the log curve to the left of one must be taken with a minus sign. The exponential curve is always above the axis, so its areas are simply integrals.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: an exponential region
slides.body_md: Find the area between $y = e^x - 1$ and the $x$-axis from $x = 0$ to $x = \log 4$.

visual.alt: Worked example table: e to the x minus 1 is not negative for x at least 0, so the area from 0 to log 4 is e to the x minus x evaluated between the limits, which is 4 minus log 4 minus 1, that is 3 minus 2 log 2.
visual.caption: Checked by quadrature.

slides.narration: For x at least zero, e to the x is at least one, so the curve is above the axis. Integrate e to the x minus one: the antiderivative is e to the x minus x. At log four it is four minus log four; at zero it is one. The area is three minus log four, that is three minus two log two.

slides.heading: Circles and ellipses
slides.body_md: Use the upper half $y = \dfrac{b}{a}\sqrt{a^2 - x^2}$ and multiply the first-quadrant area by $4$.

visual.alt: The ellipse x squared over 16 plus y squared over 4 equals 1 drawn as an upper and a lower half. It is 8 units wide and 4 units tall, passing through (0, 2) and (0, minus 2).
visual.caption: Semi-axes $4$ and $2$: area $4 \int_0^4 \tfrac12\sqrt{16 - x^2}\,dx = 8\pi$.

slides.narration: A circle or an ellipse is symmetric about both axes, so find the area in the first quadrant and multiply by four. Solve the equation for the upper half, then use the standard integral of the square root of a squared minus x squared. For an ellipse with semi-axes a and b the result is pi a b.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: area of an ellipse
slides.body_md: Using integration, find the area enclosed by $\dfrac{x^2}{25} + \dfrac{y^2}{9} = 1$.

visual.alt: Worked example table for the ellipse x squared over 25 plus y squared over 9 equals 1: the upper half is y equals three fifths of the root of 25 minus x squared; by symmetry the area is 4 times three fifths times the integral from 0 to 5, which is 25 pi over 4, giving 15 pi.
visual.caption: Matches $\pi ab = \pi \cdot 5 \cdot 3$.

slides.narration: Solve for the upper half: y equals three fifths of the square root of twenty five minus x squared. By symmetry the area is four times three fifths times the integral from zero to five. That integral is a quarter of the circle of radius five, twenty five pi over four. Multiplying gives fifteen pi.

slides.heading: Quick check: true or false?
slides.body_md: Decide whether an elliptical frame encloses a stated area.
slides.narration: Read off the two semi-axes and multiply by pi.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Below the axis: take the absolute value
Crossing the axis: split at the zeros

nodes.label: Check the sign or choose the strip

visual.alt: Summary flow for Part 1: sketch the region, find the limits, check the sign of the curve or choose the strip, then integrate and add the absolute values of the pieces.
visual.caption: Part 1 in one line.

slides.narration: To sum up. Sketch the region and find the limits. Where the curve is above the axis the area is the integral; where it is below, take the absolute value; where it crosses, split at the zeros and add the pieces. For circles and ellipses, use symmetry and the standard square root integral.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Always sketch and mark the limits
Never let pieces cancel across a zero
Give the answer in square units

rows: zeros found 1, pieces with signs 1, total 1
upper half and symmetry 1, standard integral 1, value 1
integrating across a zero and letting the pieces cancel

visual.alt: Exam tips table for Part 1: an area under a curve earns marks for the integral and the value; a curve crossing the axis earns marks for the zeros, the signed pieces and the total; a circle or ellipse earns marks for the half and the symmetry, the standard integral and the value; the common slip is letting pieces cancel across a zero.
visual.caption: A sketch earns nothing by itself but prevents most errors.

slides.narration: In the examination, draw a rough sketch first and mark the limits on it. Never integrate straight across a zero of the curve, because the pieces cancel. When you use symmetry, say so. And remember that an area is a positive number of square units.

decks.title: Application of Integrals — Part 2: Area between two curves
goals: Find the points where two curves meet and use them as limits
Decide which curve is upper and integrate upper minus lower
Split the interval where the curves cross
Find areas of regions bounded by curves, lines and circles

slides.heading: Application of Integrals, Part 2
slides.body_md: The area between two curves is the integral of the upper curve minus the lower curve.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 2: find where the curves meet, decide which is upper, integrate upper minus lower, split where they cross, and handle curves with lines and circles.
visual.caption: Part 2 at a glance.

slides.narration: Welcome to part two. Now the region is trapped between two curves. The plan is always the same: find where the curves meet, decide which one is on top, and integrate the difference. When the curves cross inside the interval, split there.

slides.heading: What you will learn

rows: Test one point between the limits
If they cross inside $[a, b]$, split there

visual.alt: Table of the four steps for the area between two curves: solve f of x equals g of x for the limits; test one point to see which curve is upper; integrate upper minus lower; split the interval wherever the curves cross.
visual.caption: Area between curves = integral of (upper − lower).

slides.narration: Here are the four steps. Solve f of x equals g of x to get the meeting points. Test one point in between to see which curve is upper. Integrate upper minus lower between the meeting points. If the curves cross inside the interval, split the interval there.

slides.heading: A lens between a parabola and a line
slides.body_md: Area $= \displaystyle\int_a^b \big(f(x) - g(x)\big)\,dx$ when $f \ge g$ on $[a, b]$.

visual.alt: Graphs of the parabola y equals x squared and the line y equals 2 x on minus 0.5 to 2.5. They meet at (0, 0) and (2, 4); between these points the line lies above the parabola, enclosing a lens.
visual.caption: Area of the lens: $\int_0^2 (2x - x^2)\,dx = \tfrac43$.

slides.narration: Each vertical strip now reaches from the lower curve up to the upper curve, so its height is f minus g. The parabola y equals x squared and the line y equals two x meet at zero and two, and the line is on top in between. The lens has area four thirds.

slides.heading: Worked example 5: parabola and line
slides.body_md: Find the area between $y = x^2$ and $y = x + 2$.

visual.alt: Worked example table for the region between y equals x squared and y equals x plus 2: they meet at minus 1 and 2; the line is above; the area is the integral of x plus 2 minus x squared from minus 1 to 2, which is 9 over 2.
visual.caption: Checked by quadrature.

slides.narration: Solve x squared equals x plus two: the curves meet at minus one and two. At zero the line gives two and the parabola gives zero, so the line is upper. Integrate x plus two minus x squared from minus one to two to get nine halves.

slides.heading: Quick check: a line and a cubic
slides.body_md: Find the first-quadrant area between a line and a cubic.
slides.narration: Which is upper between zero and one?

slides.heading: When the curves cross
slides.body_md: The upper curve changes at a crossing, so split the interval there.

visual.alt: Graphs of y equals sin x and y equals cos x from 0 to about 1.6. Cosine starts higher at 1, sine starts at 0, and they cross at x equals pi by 4, after which sine is higher.
visual.caption: Split at the crossing: the upper curve changes there.

slides.narration: Sine and cosine cross at pi by four. Before the crossing cosine is upper; after it, sine is upper. If you integrated one fixed difference over the whole interval, the two parts would partly cancel. Split at the crossing and integrate upper minus lower on each part.

slides.heading: Worked example 6: two power curves
slides.body_md: Find the area between $y = x^2$ and $y = x^3$.

visual.alt: Worked example table for the region between y equals x squared and y equals x cubed: they meet at 0 and 1; on that interval x squared is the upper curve; the area is one third minus one quarter, that is 1 over 12.
visual.caption: Test a point to decide the upper curve.

slides.narration: The curves meet where x cubed equals x squared, at zero and one. At one half, x squared is one quarter and x cubed is one eighth, so x squared is upper. The area is one third minus one quarter, that is one twelfth.

slides.heading: Quick check: root and parabola
slides.body_md: Find the area between a root curve and a parabola.
slides.narration: Integrate the square root minus x squared from zero to one.

slides.heading: A circle and a parabola
slides.body_md: Find the meeting points, then split where the boundary changes from one curve to the other.

visual.alt: The circle x squared plus y squared equals 8, drawn as two halves, and the parabola y squared equals 2 x, drawn as two branches. They meet at (2, 2) and (2, minus 2). The region inside both is bounded by the parabola up to x equals 2 and by the circle beyond it.
visual.caption: Common region: $2\pi + \tfrac43$ (Section D question).

slides.narration: Sometimes the boundary of the region is made of different curves on different parts. Inside both the circle and the parabola, the boundary is the parabola up to x equals two and the circle beyond it. So split at two, integrate each part, and use symmetry about the x-axis.

slides.heading: Worked example 7: a circular segment
slides.body_md: Find the area of the smaller segment cut from $x^2 + y^2 = 4$ by the line $x + y = 2$.

rows: Quarter circle minus the triangle under the chord

visual.alt: Worked example table for the smaller segment cut from the circle x squared plus y squared equals 4 by the line x plus y equals 2: they meet at (2, 0) and (0, 2); the segment is the quarter circle of area pi minus the triangle of area 2, so pi minus 2.
visual.caption: Checked by quadrature.

slides.narration: The line meets the circle at two, zero and at zero, two. The smaller segment lies between the arc and the chord in the first quadrant. Its area is the quarter circle, pi, minus the triangle under the chord, two. By integration, integrate the circle minus the line from zero to two.

slides.heading: An exponential curve and a line
slides.body_md: The region above a curve and below a horizontal line is also upper minus lower.

visual.alt: Graph of y equals e to the x from 0 to 1.3 and the horizontal line y equals e. The curve starts at (0, 1) and meets the line at (1, e); between x equals 0 and 1 the line is above the curve.
visual.caption: Region above the curve: $\int_0^1 (e - e^x)\,dx = 1$.

slides.narration: Here the region lies above the exponential curve and below the line y equals e. They meet at x equals one. The line is upper, so integrate e minus e to the x from zero to one. The answer is exactly one.

slides.heading: Worked example 8: using symmetry
slides.body_md: Find the area between $y = 4 - x^2$ and $y = |x| + 2$.

rows: Both curves are even: double the right half

visual.alt: Worked example table for the region between y equals 4 minus x squared and y equals the modulus of x plus 2: solving in the modulus of x gives x equals plus or minus 1; both curves are even, so the area is twice the integral of 2 minus x minus x squared from 0 to 1, which is 7 over 3.
visual.caption: Solve in $|x|$ first.

slides.narration: Because of the modulus, solve in the modulus of x: it gives the modulus of x equal to one, so the curves meet at plus and minus one. Both curves are even, so find the area on zero to one and double it. Two times seven sixths is seven thirds.

slides.heading: Quick check: do they meet?
slides.body_md: Decide whether an exponential and a logarithmic curve enclose a region.
slides.narration: Compare each curve with the line y equals x.

slides.heading: Choosing the set-up
slides.body_md: Look for crossings and for the easier direction of slicing.

nodes.label: Do the curves cross inside the interval?
Is the region easier in y?
Use horizontal strips: right minus left
Use vertical strips: upper minus lower

visual.alt: Decision flow: if the curves cross inside the interval, split at each crossing; then, if the region is easier to describe in y, use horizontal strips, right minus left; otherwise use vertical strips, upper minus lower.
visual.caption: Choosing the set-up.

slides.narration: Before integrating, ask two questions. Do the curves cross inside the interval? If so, split at each crossing. Is the region easier to describe in terms of y? If so, use horizontal strips, right minus left. Otherwise use vertical strips, upper minus lower.

slides.heading: Quick check: crossing points
slides.body_md: Count the crossing points of a cubic and a line.
slides.narration: Factorise x cubed minus four x.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Use symmetry when both curves are even

visual.alt: Summary flow for Part 2: the meeting points give the limits, integrate upper minus lower, split wherever the curves cross, and use symmetry to halve the work.
visual.caption: Part 2 in one line.

slides.narration: To sum up. The meeting points of the curves give the limits. The area is the integral of upper minus lower. Where the curves cross inside the interval, split and take upper minus lower on each part. When the region is symmetric, find half and double it.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Show the equation for the meeting points
Say which curve is upper and why

rows: meeting points 1, integrand upper minus lower 1, value 1
meeting points, correct split, two integrals, value
often (a) meeting points or a sketch, (b) the area
subtracting in the wrong order and getting a negative area

visual.alt: Exam tips table for Part 2: the area between curves earns marks for the meeting points, the integrand and the value; curve and circle questions also need the correct split; long questions often ask first for meeting points and then for the area; the common slip is a negative area from subtracting the wrong way.
visual.caption: An area is never negative.

slides.narration: In the examination, show the equation you solve for the meeting points, and say which curve is upper, for example by testing a point. Split at every crossing. If you get a negative area, you subtracted in the wrong order.

notes.title: Application of Integrals — chapter notes

sections.heading: 1. Area under a curve
sections.body_md:
If $f$ is continuous and $f(x) \ge 0$ on $[a, b]$, the area of the region bounded by $y = f(x)$, the $x$-axis and the ordinates $x = a$ and $x = b$ is $\displaystyle\int_a^b f(x)\,dx$.

Think of thin vertical strips of width $dx$ and height $f(x)$; the integral adds them up.

Always sketch the region first and mark the limits.

key_terms.definition_md: A vertical line x = a used as a boundary of the region.
A thin rectangle of width dx (or dy) used to build up the area.

visual.alt: Graph of y equals x squared over 2 plus 1 on minus 0.5 to 3.2. The curve stays above the x-axis, starting at (0, 1) and passing through (2, 3); the region under it between x equal to 0 and x equal to 2 is the area being measured.
visual.caption: Area from $x = 0$ to $x = 2$: $\int_0^2 \left(\tfrac{x^2}{2} + 1\right)dx = \tfrac{10}{3}$.

visuals.alt: Worked example table: the curve y equals x squared plus 2 x is above the axis on 0 to 2, so the area is the integral of x squared plus 2 x from 0 to 2, which is 8 over 3 plus 4, that is 20 over 3.
visuals.caption: Checked by quadrature.

sections.heading: 2. Curves below or crossing the axis
sections.body_md:
If $f(x) \le 0$ on $[a, b]$, the area is $-\displaystyle\int_a^b f(x)\,dx$.

If the curve crosses the axis inside $[a, b]$, find its zeros, split the interval there, and add the **absolute values** of the pieces. Integrating straight across a zero lets the pieces cancel and gives a wrong (too small, or even zero) answer: for example $\displaystyle\int_0^{2\pi} \sin x\,dx = 0$, but the area is $4$.

key_terms.definition_md: The value of the integral, which counts regions below the axis as negative.

visual.alt: Graph of y equals x squared minus 2 x on minus 0.5 to 3. It meets the x-axis at (0, 0) and (2, 0) and dips below the axis between them; it rises to (3, 3).
visual.caption: The dip has area $\left|\int_0^2 (x^2 - 2x)\,dx\right| = \tfrac43$.

visuals.alt: Worked example table: y equals x squared minus x minus 2 is negative on 0 to 2 and positive on 2 to 3. The areas of the two pieces are 10 over 3 and 11 over 6, adding to 31 over 6.
visuals.caption: Split at the zero $x = 2$.

sections.heading: 3. Horizontal strips; modulus, exponential and logarithmic curves
sections.body_md:
- **Horizontal strips:** for $x = g(y) \ge 0$ between $y = c$ and $y = d$, area $= \displaystyle\int_c^d g(y)\,dy$. In general, length of strip $=$ right $x$ $-$ left $x$.
- **Modulus:** split at the corner where the inside is zero; each piece is a line, so the region is made of triangles or trapeziums.
- **Exponential:** $e^x > 0$ and $a^x > 0$, so the curve is always above the axis; $\displaystyle\int a^x\,dx = \dfrac{a^x}{\log a}$.
- **Logarithmic:** $\log x < 0$ on $(0, 1)$; $\displaystyle\int \log x\,dx = x\log x - x$.

key_terms.definition_md: A thin rectangle of height dy whose length is right x minus left x.

visual.alt: Table comparing strips: a vertical strip of width d x has length upper y minus lower y; a horizontal strip of width d y has length right x minus left x. Example: between x equals y squared and the y-axis for y from 0 to 2 the area is 8 over 3.
visual.caption: Choose the strip that gives one formula for the whole region.

visuals.alt: Graph of y equals the modulus of x plus 1 on minus 3.2 to 2.2: a V shape with its corner at (minus 1, 0), rising to (minus 3, 2) on the left and to (2, 3) on the right.
visuals.caption: Two triangles: $2 + 4.5 = 6.5$ square units.

visuals.alt: Graph of y equals log x for x from 0.25 to 4. It is below the x-axis for x less than 1, crosses the axis at (1, 0), and passes through (e, 1).
visuals.caption: From $x = 1$ to $x = e$ the area is $1$; to the left of $1$ the curve is below the axis.

visuals.alt: Worked example table: e to the x minus 1 is not negative for x at least 0, so the area from 0 to log 4 is e to the x minus x evaluated between the limits, which is 4 minus log 4 minus 1, that is 3 minus 2 log 2.
visuals.caption: Checked by quadrature.

sections.heading: 4. Circles and ellipses
sections.body_md:
For $\dfrac{x^2}{a^2} + \dfrac{y^2}{b^2} = 1$, the upper half is $y = \dfrac{b}{a}\sqrt{a^2 - x^2}$. By symmetry about both axes,

Area $= 4 \cdot \dfrac{b}{a}\displaystyle\int_0^a \sqrt{a^2 - x^2}\,dx = 4 \cdot \dfrac{b}{a} \cdot \dfrac{\pi a^2}{4} = \pi ab$.

A circle of radius $r$ is the case $a = b = r$, giving $\pi r^2$. Parts of a circle (between two ordinates) use the standard integral directly.

key_terms.definition_md: The numbers a and b in the standard equation of an ellipse: half its width and half its height.

visual.alt: The ellipse x squared over 16 plus y squared over 4 equals 1 drawn as an upper and a lower half. It is 8 units wide and 4 units tall, passing through (0, 2) and (0, minus 2).
visual.caption: Semi-axes $4$ and $2$: area $4 \int_0^4 \tfrac12\sqrt{16 - x^2}\,dx = 8\pi$.

visuals.alt: Worked example table for the ellipse x squared over 25 plus y squared over 9 equals 1: the upper half is y equals three fifths of the root of 25 minus x squared; by symmetry the area is 4 times three fifths times the integral from 0 to 5, which is 25 pi over 4, giving 15 pi.
visuals.caption: Matches $\pi ab = \pi \cdot 5 \cdot 3$.

sections.heading: 5. Area between two curves
sections.body_md:
If $f(x) \ge g(x)$ on $[a, b]$, the area between the curves is $\displaystyle\int_a^b \big(f(x) - g(x)\big)\,dx$; this holds even if part of the region is below the $x$-axis.

**Steps:** solve $f(x) = g(x)$ for the meeting points; test one point to decide which curve is upper; integrate upper minus lower. If the curves cross inside the interval, split there and take upper minus lower on each part.

key_terms.definition_md: The x-values where f(x) = g(x); they are the limits of the integral.
The curve with the larger y-value at every x of the interval.

visual.alt: Graphs of the parabola y equals x squared and the line y equals 2 x on minus 0.5 to 2.5. They meet at (0, 0) and (2, 4); between these points the line lies above the parabola, enclosing a lens.
visual.caption: Area of the lens: $\int_0^2 (2x - x^2)\,dx = \tfrac43$.

visuals.alt: Worked example table for the region between y equals x squared and y equals x plus 2: they meet at minus 1 and 2; the line is above; the area is the integral of x plus 2 minus x squared from minus 1 to 2, which is 9 over 2.
visuals.caption: Checked by quadrature.

sections.heading: 6. Regions bounded by curves, lines and circles
sections.body_md:
- A **segment** of a circle or ellipse cut off by a chord is the area under the arc minus the area under the chord.
- When the boundary of the region changes from one curve to another (for example the region inside both a circle and a parabola), split at the meeting point and integrate each part.
- Use **symmetry**: if both curves are even, find the area for $x \ge 0$ and double it; for a region symmetric about the $x$-axis, double the upper half.
- Regions described by inequalities, such as $\{(x, y) : x^2 \le y \le |x|\}$, are read as "lower curve $\le y \le$ upper curve".

notes.exam_tips_md:
**How ISC marks are awarded**
- *Area under a curve (2 marks):* the correct integral, then the value.
- *Curve crossing the axis (3 marks):* the zeros, the pieces with the correct signs, the total.
- *Area between curves (3 marks):* the meeting points, upper minus lower, the value.
- *Section D (5 marks):* often (a) the meeting points or a sketch and (b) the area, sometimes with a circle or an ellipse.

**Common mistakes**
- Integrating across a zero so that the pieces cancel.
- Subtracting lower minus upper and reporting a negative area.
- Forgetting the lower half of a region symmetric about the $x$-axis.
- Using the wrong limits for a horizontal strip (they must be values of $y$).

questions.stem_md: A flower bed in an imagined Shimla garden is the region under the line $y = 3x + 1$ above the $x$-axis between $x = 0$ and $x = 2$ (lengths in metres). Its area is
questions.solution_md: $\displaystyle\int_0^2 (3x + 1)\,dx = \left[\dfrac{3x^2}{2} + x\right]_0^2 = 6 + 2 = 8$. Option (c) leaves out the constant term.

questions.stem_md: The cubic $y = x^3$ is drawn for $0 \le x \le 2$. The area between this arc, the $x$-axis and the ordinate $x = 2$ is
questions.solution_md: $\displaystyle\int_0^2 x^3\,dx = \dfrac{2^4}{4} = 4$.

questions.stem_md: The parabola $y = x^2 - 4$ dips below the $x$-axis between its zeros $\pm 2$. The area of the region trapped between this dip and the axis is
questions.solution_md: The integral $\displaystyle\int_{-2}^{2} (x^2 - 4)\,dx = -\dfrac{32}{3}$ is negative because the curve is below the axis; the area is its absolute value, $\dfrac{32}{3}$.

questions.stem_md: Under the exponential curve $y = e^x$, from the $y$-axis to the line $x = \log 3$, the enclosed area (above the $x$-axis) is
questions.solution_md: $\displaystyle\int_0^{\log 3} e^x\,dx = e^{\log 3} - e^0 = 3 - 1 = 2$.

questions.stem_md: The logarithmic curve $y = \log x$ rises from the point $(1, 0)$. The region between this curve, the $x$-axis and the line $x = e$ has area
questions.solution_md: $\displaystyle\int_1^e \log x\,dx = [x\log x - x]_1^e = (e - e) - (0 - 1) = 1$.

questions.stem_md: A rectangular hyperbola $y = \dfrac{1}{x}$ is sketched for $x > 0$. The area under it between the ordinates $x = 1$ and $x = 4$ is
questions.solution_md: $\displaystyle\int_1^4 \dfrac{dx}{x} = \log 4 = 2\log 2$.

questions.stem_md: Only the first-quadrant quarter of the disc bounded by $x^2 + y^2 = 8$ is shaded on a logo. The shaded area is
questions.solution_md: $\displaystyle\int_0^{2\sqrt2} \sqrt{8 - x^2}\,dx = \dfrac14 \cdot 8\pi = 2\pi$.

questions.stem_md: A running-track infield is modelled by the ellipse $\dfrac{x^2}{9} + \dfrac{y^2}{36} = 1$. The area it encloses is
questions.solution_md: An ellipse with semi-axes $a$ and $b$ encloses $\pi ab$; here $\pi \cdot 3 \cdot 6 = 18\pi$.

questions.stem_md: The V-shaped graph of $y = |2x - 3|$ touches the $x$-axis at $x = \dfrac32$. The total area between this graph and the $x$-axis for $0 \le x \le 3$ is
questions.solution_md: Two triangles, each with base $\dfrac32$ and height $3$: $2 \times \dfrac12 \cdot \dfrac32 \cdot 3 = \dfrac92$. Option (b) integrates $2x - 3$ without the modulus.

questions.stem_md: Over one full wave, $0 \le x \le 2\pi$, the sine curve and the $x$-axis enclose two humps. Their total area is
questions.solution_md: $\displaystyle\int_0^{2\pi} \sin x\,dx = 0$ because the second hump is below the axis. The area is $2\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi} \sin x\,dx = 4$.

questions.stem_md: The parabola $y^2 = 8x$ opens to the right. The region it cuts off with the vertical line $x = 2$ (above and below the axis) has area
questions.solution_md: By symmetry the area is $2\displaystyle\int_0^2 \sqrt{8x}\,dx = 2\sqrt8 \cdot \dfrac23 \cdot 2^{3/2} = \dfrac{32}{3}$. Option (d) counts only the upper half.

questions.stem_md: Horizontal strips are natural for the sideways parabola $x = 9 - y^2$. The region between this curve and the $y$-axis has area
questions.solution_md: The curve meets the $y$-axis at $y = \pm 3$. Area $= \displaystyle\int_{-3}^{3} (9 - y^2)\,dy = 54 - 18 = 36$.

questions.stem_md: The quadratic curve $y = x^2 - 3x$ forms a single loop below the $x$-axis between $x = 0$ and $x = 3$. The area of the loop is
questions.solution_md: $\displaystyle\int_0^3 (3x - x^2)\,dx = \dfrac{27}{2} - 9 = \dfrac92$. An area is never negative, so option (b) is wrong.

questions.stem_md: Between $x = 0$ and $x = 2$, the region under the exponential curve $y = 2^x$ and above the $x$-axis has area
questions.solution_md: $\displaystyle\int_0^2 2^x\,dx = \left[\dfrac{2^x}{\log 2}\right]_0^2 = \dfrac{4 - 1}{\log 2} = \dfrac{3}{\log 2}$.

questions.stem_md: A leaf-shaped badge is the region between the parabola $y = x^2$ and the line $y = 2x$. Its area is
questions.solution_md: They meet where $x^2 = 2x$: $x = 0, 2$. Area $= \displaystyle\int_0^2 (2x - x^2)\,dx = 4 - \dfrac83 = \dfrac43$.

questions.stem_md: In the first quadrant the line $y = x$ lies above the cubic $y = x^3$ until they meet again at $x = 1$. The area between them there is
questions.solution_md: $\displaystyle\int_0^1 (x - x^3)\,dx = \dfrac12 - \dfrac14 = \dfrac14$.

questions.stem_md: The line $y = x$ cuts the parabola $y = x^2 - 2$ at $x = -1$ and $x = 2$. The area of the region between them is
questions.solution_md: $\displaystyle\int_{-1}^{2} (x - x^2 + 2)\,dx = \left[\dfrac{x^2}{2} - \dfrac{x^3}{3} + 2x\right]_{-1}^{2} = \dfrac{10}{3} + \dfrac76 = \dfrac92$.

questions.stem_md: Between $x = 0$ and $x = 1$ the root curve $y = \sqrt{x}$ lies above the parabola $y = x^2$. The area between the two is
questions.solution_md: $\displaystyle\int_0^1 (\sqrt{x} - x^2)\,dx = \dfrac23 - \dfrac13 = \dfrac13$.

questions.stem_md: For $0 \le x \le 1$ the exponential curve $y = e^x$ rises above the horizontal line $y = 1$. The area of the sliver between them is
questions.solution_md: $\displaystyle\int_0^1 (e^x - 1)\,dx = (e - 1) - 1 = e - 2$.

questions.stem_md: From the $y$-axis to the line $x = \dfrac{\pi}{4}$, cosine stays above sine. The area enclosed between the two graphs there is
questions.solution_md: $\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/4} (\cos x - \sin x)\,dx = [\sin x + \cos x]_0^{\pi/4} = \sqrt2 - 1$.

questions.stem_md: A triangular kite panel is bounded above by the line $y = 2$ and below by the graph $y = |x|$. Its area is
questions.solution_md: The graphs meet at $x = \pm 2$. Area $= \displaystyle\int_{-2}^{2} (2 - |x|)\,dx = 2\int_0^2 (2 - x)\,dx = 4$.

questions.stem_md: The upper branch $y = 2\sqrt{x}$ of the parabola $y^2 = 4x$ and the line $y = 2x$ meet at the origin and at $(1, 2)$. The area between them is
questions.solution_md: $\displaystyle\int_0^1 (2\sqrt{x} - 2x)\,dx = \dfrac43 - 1 = \dfrac13$.

questions.stem_md: Before finding the area between the cubic $y = x^3$ and the line $y = 4x$, a student lists the points where they cross. How many such points are there?
questions.solution_md: $x^3 = 4x$ gives $x(x^2 - 4) = 0$, so $x = 0$ and $x = \pm 2$: three points.

questions.stem_md: The cubic $y = x^3$ and the line $y = 4x$ enclose two congruent loops, one on each side of the origin. Their total area is
questions.solution_md: By symmetry the total is $2\displaystyle\int_0^2 (4x - x^3)\,dx = 2(8 - 4) = 8$. Integrating $4x - x^3$ from $-2$ to $2$ gives $0$ (option c), because the loops cancel.

questions.stem_md: A pond outline is formed by the line $y = \dfrac52 - x$ and the hyperbola $y = \dfrac1x$, which meet at $x = \dfrac12$ and $x = 2$. The area of the pond is
questions.solution_md: $\displaystyle\int_{1/2}^{2} \left(\dfrac52 - x - \dfrac1x\right)dx = \dfrac52 \cdot \dfrac32 - \dfrac{4 - \tfrac14}{2} - \log 4 = \dfrac{15}{8} - 2\log 2$.

questions.stem_md: The chord $\dfrac{x}{4} + \dfrac{y}{3} = 1$ cuts a small cap off the first-quadrant part of the ellipse $\dfrac{x^2}{16} + \dfrac{y^2}{9} = 1$. The area of that cap is
questions.solution_md: Quarter ellipse $\dfrac14 \pi \cdot 4 \cdot 3 = 3\pi$ minus the triangle under the chord, $\dfrac12 \cdot 4 \cdot 3 = 6$: the cap is $3\pi - 6$.

**Reason (R):** For the part of a curve below the $x$-axis, the area is the absolute value of the integral over that part.

**Assertion (A):** The ellipse $\dfrac{x^2}{a^2} + \dfrac{y^2}{b^2} = 1$ encloses an area of $\pi ab$.

**Reason (R):** The ellipse is symmetric about both coordinate axes.

**Assertion (A):** The area between $y = x^2$ and $y = x$ for $0 \le x \le 1$ is $\displaystyle\int_0^1 (x^2 - x)\,dx = -\dfrac16$.

**Reason (R):** If $g(x) \ge f(x)$ on $[a, b]$, the area between the curves is $\displaystyle\int_a^b \big(g(x) - f(x)\big)\,dx$.

Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The region between $y = \log x$, the $x$-axis and the lines $x = \dfrac1e$ and $x = 1$ has area $1 - \dfrac{2}{e}$.

**Reason (R):** $\log x < 0$ for $0 < x < 1$.

Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.

questions.solution_md: On $\left[\dfrac1e, 1\right]$ the curve is below the axis (R), so the area is $-\displaystyle\int_{1/e}^{1} \log x\,dx = -\left[x\log x - x\right]_{1/e}^{1} = 1 - \dfrac2e$. R explains why the sign is reversed.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The disc $x^2 + y^2 \le r^2$ has area $4\displaystyle\int_0^r \sqrt{r^2 - x^2}\,dx = \pi r^2$.

**Reason (R):** The circle $x^2 + y^2 = r^2$ is symmetric only about the $x$-axis.

options.text_md: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

questions.solution_md: A is true: the first-quadrant integral is $\dfrac{\pi r^2}{4}$. R is false: the circle is symmetric about both axes (indeed about every line through the centre), which is why the factor $4$ is allowed.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The parabolas $y = x^2$ and $y = 2 - x^2$ enclose a region of area $\dfrac83$.

**Reason (R):** The two parabolas meet at $x = -1$ and $x = 1$.

options.text_md: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

questions.solution_md: Both are true: $\displaystyle\int_{-1}^{1} (2 - 2x^2)\,dx = 4 - \dfrac43 = \dfrac83$. Knowing the meeting points only gives the limits; it does not by itself explain the value $\dfrac83$.

questions.stem_md: True or false: if a continuous curve $y = f(x)$ lies wholly below the $x$-axis on $[a, b]$, the area between it and the axis equals $-\displaystyle\int_a^b f(x)\,dx$.
questions.solution_md: The integral is negative there, so its negative is the (positive) area.

questions.stem_md: True or false: the area bounded by the line $y = x - 1$, the $x$-axis and the lines $x = 0$ and $x = 2$ is $\displaystyle\int_0^2 (x - 1)\,dx$.
questions.solution_md: That integral is $0$, because the triangle below the axis cancels the one above. The area is $\dfrac12 + \dfrac12 = 1$.

questions.stem_md: True or false: a mirror frame shaped like the ellipse $\dfrac{x^2}{4} + \dfrac{y^2}{25} = 1$ encloses exactly $10\pi$ square units.
questions.solution_md: Semi-axes $2$ and $5$: $\pi \cdot 2 \cdot 5 = 10\pi$.

questions.stem_md: True or false: the curves $y = e^x$ and $y = \log x$ cross at some point, so a bounded region lies between them.
questions.solution_md: For $x > 0$, $e^x > x > \log x$ (since $e^x \ge 1 + x$ and $\log x \le x - 1$), so the curves never meet and enclose no bounded region.

questions.stem_md: The region under $y = 6x^2$ from $x = 0$ to $x = k$ (with $k > 0$) has area $16$. Then $k =$ ____.
questions.solution_md: $\displaystyle\int_0^k 6x^2\,dx = 2k^3 = 16$, so $k^3 = 8$ and $k = 2$.

questions.stem_md: A round table top is modelled by $x^2 + y^2 = 7$. Its area is $k\pi$ square units, where $k =$ ____.
questions.solution_md: Radius $\sqrt7$, so the area is $7\pi$.

questions.stem_md: The parabolic arch $y = 4 - x^2$ and the ground line $y = 0$ enclose ____ square units.
A lawn edge follows $y = x^2 + 1$ (metres). Find the area under it, above the $x$-axis, between $x = 0$ and $x = 3$, in square metres.
questions.solution_md: $\displaystyle\int_0^3 (x^2 + 1)\,dx = 9 + 3 = 12$.

questions.stem_md: The parabolas $y = x^2$ and $y = 6x - x^2$ meet at $x = 0$ and $x = 3$. Find the area of the lens between them.
questions.solution_md: $\displaystyle\int_0^3 (6x - 2x^2)\,dx = 27 - 18 = 9$.

questions.stem_md: Find the total area between the graph of $y = |x + 1|$ and the $x$-axis for $-3 \le x \le 2$.
questions.solution_md: Two triangles meeting at $x = -1$: $\dfrac12 \cdot 2 \cdot 2 + \dfrac12 \cdot 3 \cdot 3 = 2 + 4.5 = 6.5$.

questions.stem_md: Find the area under the curve $y = e^{2x}$, above the $x$-axis, from $x = 0$ to $x = \log 2$.
The oval $9x^2 + 4y^2 = 36$ encloses $k\pi$ square units. Find $k$.
questions.solution_md: In standard form $\dfrac{x^2}{4} + \dfrac{y^2}{9} = 1$: semi-axes $2$ and $3$, so the area is $6\pi$ and $k = 6$.

questions.stem_md: The cubic $y = x^3 - x$ crosses the $x$-axis at $-1$, $0$ and $1$. Find the total area of its two loops with the axis on $[-1, 1]$.
questions.solution_md: Each loop has area $\displaystyle\int_0^1 (x - x^3)\,dx = \dfrac14$, so the total is $0.5$.

questions.stem_md: A vegetable bed in an imagined school garden at Dehradun is bounded by the curve $y = 2\sqrt{x}$, the $x$-axis and the line $x = 4$ (metres). Find its area.

answer.model_answer_md: Area $= \displaystyle\int_0^4 2\sqrt{x}\,dx = 2 \cdot \dfrac23 \left[x^{3/2}\right]_0^4 = \dfrac43 \cdot 8 = \dfrac{32}{3}$ m$^2$.

questions.solution_md: Integrate the curve between the limits.

questions.stem_md: Find the area under the curve $y = \dfrac{3}{x}$, above the $x$-axis, between the ordinates $x = 1$ and $x = e^2$.

answer.model_answer_md: Area $= \displaystyle\int_1^{e^2} \dfrac{3}{x}\,dx = 3\left[\log x\right]_1^{e^2} = 3 \cdot 2 = 6$.

questions.solution_md: The antiderivative of 3/x is 3 log x.

questions.stem_md: The curve $y = x^2 - 1$ crosses the $x$-axis at $x = 1$. Find the area between this curve and the $x$-axis from $x = 0$ to $x = 2$.

answer.model_answer_md:
On $[0, 1]$ the curve is below the axis: $\displaystyle\int_0^1 (1 - x^2)\,dx = \dfrac23$.

On $[1, 2]$ it is above: $\displaystyle\int_1^2 (x^2 - 1)\,dx = \dfrac43$.

Total area $= \dfrac23 + \dfrac43 = 2$.

questions.solution_md: Split at the zero x = 1 and add absolute values.

questions.stem_md: A semicircular stage front is bounded by $x^2 + y^2 = 18$ with $y \ge 0$. Find the area of the part of the stage between the lines $x = 0$ and $x = 3$.

answer.model_answer_md:
Area $= \displaystyle\int_0^3 \sqrt{18 - x^2}\,dx = \left[\dfrac{x}{2}\sqrt{18 - x^2} + 9\sin^{-1}\dfrac{x}{3\sqrt2}\right]_0^3$

$= \dfrac32 \cdot 3 + 9 \cdot \dfrac{\pi}{4} = \dfrac92 + \dfrac{9\pi}{4}$.

questions.solution_md: Use the standard integral of the square root of a² − x².

questions.stem_md: The line $y = 3x$ and the parabola $y = x^2$ meet at the origin and at $(3, 9)$. Find the area of the region between them.

answer.model_answer_md:
On $[0, 3]$, $3x \ge x^2$.

Area $= \displaystyle\int_0^3 (3x - x^2)\,dx = \dfrac{27}{2} - 9 = \dfrac92$.

questions.solution_md: Upper minus lower between the meeting points.

questions.stem_md: Find the area of the single arch of the cosine curve that lies between $x = 0$ and $x = \pi$, counting the part below the axis as positive.

answer.model_answer_md:
$\cos x \ge 0$ on $\left[0, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right]$ and $\le 0$ on $\left[\dfrac{\pi}{2}, \pi\right]$.

Area $= \displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/2} \cos x\,dx - \int_{\pi/2}^{\pi} \cos x\,dx = 1 + 1 = 2$.

questions.solution_md: Split at π/2.

questions.stem_md: A tunnel mouth is the region between the arch $y = 5 - x^2$ and the sloping track $y = x - 1$. Given that they meet at $x = -3$ and $x = 2$, find its area.

answer.model_answer_md:
On $[-3, 2]$ the arch is above the track.

Area $= \displaystyle\int_{-3}^{2} (6 - x - x^2)\,dx = \left[6x - \dfrac{x^2}{2} - \dfrac{x^3}{3}\right]_{-3}^{2} = \dfrac{22}{3} + \dfrac{27}{2} = \dfrac{125}{6}$.

questions.solution_md: Upper minus lower, then the limits.

questions.stem_md: Find the area between the curves $y = e^x$ and $y = e^{-x}$ from their meeting point on the $y$-axis to the line $x = 1$.

answer.model_answer_md:
They meet at $(0, 1)$; for $x > 0$, $e^x > e^{-x}$.

Area $= \displaystyle\int_0^1 (e^x - e^{-x})\,dx = (e - 1) - \left(1 - \dfrac1e\right) = e + \dfrac1e - 2$.

questions.solution_md: Upper minus lower on [0, 1].

questions.stem_md: Find the area of the region between the curve $y = \log x$, the $x$-axis and the line $x = e^2$.

answer.model_answer_md:
The curve meets the axis at $x = 1$ and is above it for $x > 1$.

Area $= \displaystyle\int_1^{e^2} \log x\,dx = [x\log x - x]_1^{e^2} = (2e^2 - e^2) - (0 - 1) = e^2 + 1$.

questions.solution_md: Integrate log x by parts (standard result) from 1.

questions.stem_md: A garden pond in an imagined Bhopal park is shaped like the ellipse $\dfrac{x^2}{49} + \dfrac{y^2}{9} = 1$ (metres). Using integration, find the area of the pond.

answer.model_answer_md:
By symmetry the area is $4$ times the first-quadrant part, where $y = \dfrac37\sqrt{49 - x^2}$.

Area $= 4 \cdot \dfrac37\displaystyle\int_0^7 \sqrt{49 - x^2}\,dx = \dfrac{12}{7}\left[\dfrac{x}{2}\sqrt{49 - x^2} + \dfrac{49}{2}\sin^{-1}\dfrac{x}{7}\right]_0^7 = \dfrac{12}{7} \cdot \dfrac{49\pi}{4} = 21\pi$ m$^2$.

questions.solution_md: Four times the quarter, with the standard square-root integral.

questions.stem_md: The parabola $y^2 = 4x$ and the line $y = x$ enclose a slim region. Find the points where they meet and the area of the region.

answer.model_answer_md:
Substituting $y = x$: $x^2 = 4x$, so $x = 0$ or $x = 4$; the points are $(0, 0)$ and $(4, 4)$.

On $[0, 4]$ the branch $y = 2\sqrt{x}$ is above the line.

Area $= \displaystyle\int_0^4 (2\sqrt{x} - x)\,dx = \dfrac{32}{3} - 8 = \dfrac83$.

questions.solution_md: Meeting points, then upper branch minus line.

questions.stem_md: The line $y = x$ and the cubic $y = x^3$ cross three times. Sketch them mentally, find the crossing points, and find the total area enclosed between them.

answer.model_answer_md:
$x^3 = x$ gives $x = -1, 0, 1$.

On $[0, 1]$, $x \ge x^3$; on $[-1, 0]$, $x^3 \ge x$. Each loop has area $\displaystyle\int_0^1 (x - x^3)\,dx = \dfrac14$ (the second by symmetry about the origin).

Total area $= \dfrac12$.

questions.solution_md: Two loops; integrating x − x³ from −1 to 1 would give 0.

questions.stem_md: Find the area of the region $\{(x, y) : x^2 \le y \le |x|\}$, a pair of small petals on either side of the $y$-axis.

answer.model_answer_md:
$x^2 = |x|$ gives $x = 0$ or $|x| = 1$, so $x = -1, 0, 1$.

By symmetry about the $y$-axis, area $= 2\displaystyle\int_0^1 (x - x^2)\,dx = 2\left(\dfrac12 - \dfrac13\right) = \dfrac13$.

questions.solution_md: Use the symmetry of |x| and x².

questions.stem_md: A ramp profile is $y = |x - 1| + |x - 3|$ for $0 \le x \le 4$. Write $y$ without modulus signs on each part and find the area under the profile.
questions.solution_md: Split at the corners x = 1 and x = 3.

questions.stem_md: On a quarter-turn window $\left[0, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right]$, the graphs of $\sin x$ and $\cos x$ cross once. Find the total area enclosed between them over this interval.

answer.model_answer_md:
They cross at $x = \dfrac{\pi}{4}$.

Area $= \displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/4} (\cos x - \sin x)\,dx + \int_{\pi/4}^{\pi/2} (\sin x - \cos x)\,dx = (\sqrt2 - 1) + (\sqrt2 - 1) = 2\sqrt2 - 2$.

questions.solution_md: Split at the crossing and take upper minus lower on each part.

questions.stem_md: Find the area of the region bounded by the curve $y = e^x$, the $y$-axis and the horizontal line $y = e$, lying above the curve.

answer.model_answer_md:
The line $y = e$ meets the curve at $x = 1$.

Area $= \displaystyle\int_0^1 (e - e^x)\,dx = e - (e - 1) = 1$.

questions.solution_md: The line minus the curve on [0, 1].

questions.stem_md: Find the area of the strip between the parabola $y = x^2 + 2$ and the line $y = x$ from $x = 0$ to $x = 3$, after showing that the parabola stays above the line.

answer.model_answer_md:
$x^2 + 2 - x = \left(x - \dfrac12\right)^2 + \dfrac74 > 0$, so the parabola is always above the line.

Area $= \displaystyle\int_0^3 (x^2 - x + 2)\,dx = 9 - \dfrac92 + 6 = \dfrac{21}{2}$.

questions.solution_md: Complete the square to fix the order, then integrate.

questions.stem_md: The graph $y = |x|$ and the parabola $y = x^2 - 2$ enclose a bowl-shaped region. Find where they meet and the area of the bowl.

answer.model_answer_md:
$x^2 - 2 = |x|$ gives $|x|^2 - |x| - 2 = 0$, so $|x| = 2$ and $x = \pm 2$.

By symmetry, area $= 2\displaystyle\int_0^2 (x - x^2 + 2)\,dx = 2\left(2 - \dfrac83 + 4\right) = \dfrac{20}{3}$.

questions.solution_md: Solve in |x|, then use symmetry.

questions.stem_md: Using the substitution $t = x^2$, find the area under the curve $y = x e^{x^2}$ between $x = 0$ and $x = 1$.

answer.model_answer_md:
$dt = 2x\,dx$; the limits become $0$ and $1$.

Area $= \dfrac12\displaystyle\int_0^1 e^t\,dt = \dfrac{e - 1}{2}$.

questions.solution_md: The curve is above the axis on [0, 1]; substitute and change the limits.

questions.stem_md:
A bank of a canal in an imagined Punjab village follows $y = x^2 - 5x + 4$ for $0 \le x \le 5$, with the $x$-axis as the water line.

(a) Find where the curve meets the $x$-axis and state where it lies below the axis. [2]

(b) Find the total area enclosed between the curve and the $x$-axis over $[0, 5]$. [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** $x^2 - 5x + 4 = (x - 1)(x - 4) = 0$ at $x = 1$ and $x = 4$; the curve is below the axis on $(1, 4)$.

**(b)** With $P(x) = \dfrac{x^3}{3} - \dfrac{5x^2}{2} + 4x$: $P(0) = 0$, $P(1) = \dfrac{11}{6}$, $P(4) = -\dfrac83$, $P(5) = -\dfrac56$.

Pieces: $\dfrac{11}{6}$ on $[0, 1]$, $\left|-\dfrac83 - \dfrac{11}{6}\right| = \dfrac92$ on $[1, 4]$, $-\dfrac56 + \dfrac83 = \dfrac{11}{6}$ on $[4, 5]$.

Total area $= \dfrac{11}{6} + \dfrac{27}{6} + \dfrac{11}{6} = \dfrac{49}{6}$.

questions.solution_md: Split at the zeros and add absolute values.

questions.stem_md:
A lamp shade is modelled by the region common to the disc $x^2 + y^2 \le 8$ and the inside of the parabola $y^2 = 2x$.

(a) Find the points where the circle and the parabola meet. [2]

(b) Find the area of the common region. [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** Substituting $y^2 = 2x$: $x^2 + 2x - 8 = 0$, so $x = 2$ (the root $x = -4$ gives no real $y$). The points are $(2, 2)$ and $(2, -2)$.

**(b)** By symmetry about the $x$-axis, area $= 2\left[\displaystyle\int_0^2 \sqrt{2x}\,dx + \int_2^{2\sqrt2} \sqrt{8 - x^2}\,dx\right]$.

$\displaystyle\int_0^2 \sqrt{2x}\,dx = \dfrac83$; $\displaystyle\int_2^{2\sqrt2} \sqrt{8 - x^2}\,dx = \left[\dfrac{x}{2}\sqrt{8 - x^2} + 4\sin^{-1}\dfrac{x}{2\sqrt2}\right]_2^{2\sqrt2} = 2\pi - (2 + \pi) = \pi - 2$.

Area $= 2\left(\dfrac83 + \pi - 2\right) = 2\pi + \dfrac43$.

questions.solution_md: Parabola up to x = 2, circle beyond; double for symmetry.

questions.stem_md:
A logo is cut from the ellipse $4x^2 + 9y^2 = 36$.

(a) Using integration, find the area enclosed by the ellipse. [2]

(b) The chord $2x + 3y = 6$ cuts off a small segment of the ellipse in the first quadrant. Find the area of that segment. [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** $\dfrac{x^2}{9} + \dfrac{y^2}{4} = 1$, so $y = \dfrac23\sqrt{9 - x^2}$ in the first quadrant.

Area $= 4 \cdot \dfrac23\displaystyle\int_0^3 \sqrt{9 - x^2}\,dx = \dfrac83 \cdot \dfrac{9\pi}{4} = 6\pi$.

**(b)** The chord meets the ellipse at $(3, 0)$ and $(0, 2)$.

Segment $= \displaystyle\int_0^3 \left(\dfrac23\sqrt{9 - x^2} - \dfrac{6 - 2x}{3}\right)dx = \dfrac{3\pi}{2} - 3$.

questions.solution_md: Quarter ellipse minus the triangle under the chord.

questions.stem_md:
A cricket-pitch cover is shaped like the region between the parabola $y = x^2$ and the line $y = 2x + 8$.

(a) Find the points where the line meets the parabola. [2]

(b) Find the area of the region. [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** $x^2 = 2x + 8$ gives $x^2 - 2x - 8 = (x - 4)(x + 2) = 0$, so $x = -2$ or $x = 4$; the points are $(-2, 4)$ and $(4, 16)$.

**(b)** On $[-2, 4]$ the line is above the parabola.

Area $= \displaystyle\int_{-2}^{4} (2x + 8 - x^2)\,dx = \left[x^2 + 8x - \dfrac{x^3}{3}\right]_{-2}^{4} = \dfrac{80}{3} + \dfrac{28}{3} = 36$.

questions.solution_md: Meeting points, then line minus parabola.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Find the area under $y = \log(x + 1)$, above the $x$-axis, from $x = 0$ to $x = e - 1$. [2]

(b) The exponential curve $y = 2^x$ and the line $y = x + 1$ meet at $x = 0$ and $x = 1$. Find the area between them. [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** With $u = x + 1$: $\displaystyle\int_1^{e} \log u\,du = [u\log u - u]_1^e = 0 - (-1) = 1$.

**(b)** On $[0, 1]$ the line is above the curve (for example at $x = \dfrac12$: $1.5 > \sqrt2$).

Area $= \displaystyle\int_0^1 (x + 1 - 2^x)\,dx = \dfrac12 + 1 - \dfrac{2 - 1}{\log 2} = \dfrac32 - \dfrac{1}{\log 2}$.

questions.solution_md: Shift the variable in (a); line minus curve in (b).

questions.stem_md:
Consider the region $\{(x, y) : 0 \le y \le x^2 + 1,\ 0 \le y \le x + 1,\ 0 \le x \le 2\}$.

(a) Show that $x^2 + 1 \le x + 1$ on $[0, 1]$ and $x + 1 \le x^2 + 1$ on $[1, 2]$, so name the upper boundary on each part. [2]

(b) Find the area of the region. [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** $(x + 1) - (x^2 + 1) = x(1 - x)$, which is $\ge 0$ on $[0, 1]$ and $\le 0$ on $[1, 2]$. So the top of the region is $y = x^2 + 1$ on $[0, 1]$ and $y = x + 1$ on $[1, 2]$.

**(b)** Area $= \displaystyle\int_0^1 (x^2 + 1)\,dx + \int_1^2 (x + 1)\,dx = \dfrac43 + \dfrac52 = \dfrac{23}{6}$.

questions.solution_md: The region is under the lower of the two curves at each x.
